atlanta-holds-out-war-stalemated.summary: In this world, the voters I interviewed lean 4.9 points further toward McClellan than the same people did in 1864 as it was. Connecticut, Indiana, New Hampshire, New York and 1 more flip, but Lincoln still wins, 129–104. The closest call is Michigan, which holds for Lincoln by 0.4 points. McClellan wins in 32 of 100 draws.
assumptions: Without the September victory, war-weariness is stronger and the opposition party's claim that the war is a failure gains support among persuadable voters in the loyal states, while the soldiers' and committed partisans' behavior is largely unchanged.
howIGotThis: What changed: Atlanta remains in Confederate hands through autumn and the war appears deadlocked on Election Day.

What historians found (11 findings, strong evidence): No direct evidence on a no-Atlanta 1864. Contemporaries (Raymond, Lincoln, Weed) expected defeat in August; 1862 midterms show Northern swings to Democrats under discouraging news, though mixed with emancipation and conscription. Soldiers favored Lincoln heavily after Atlanta.
The numbers: the 1860 and 1870 census counts interpolated to 1864 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1864 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

before.quote: The war's been long and hard, but we can't make peace with the rebellion still fighting. The President's promise to end slavery for good—that's the right course, even if it takes more time.
before.reason: Harry Ellis is a 68-year-old property-owning taxpayer in Illinois, qualified to vote. As a man of working-class stability in a town during wartime, he likely favors the incumbent's commitment to unconditional victory and constitutional abolition of slavery over the opposition's call for negotiated peace, which many in the North fear would preserve slavery.

after.quote: The General talks of peace, but I fear giving up now means the boys died for nothing. Lincoln means to see it through to a proper end.
after.reason: Harry Ellis is a property-owning white man in Illinois who meets the legal requirements to vote. At 68, he has lived through the entire conflict and likely sees the war's continuation under Lincoln as necessary to preserve the Union and end slavery, while viewing the opposition candidate's peace platform with suspicion given the stalemate's toll.

before.quote: The Union must hold, and slavery must end. Four more years of fighting is better than letting the rebellion win and breaking up the country for good.
before.reason: Ernest Reed is a property-owning or tax-paying white man in Massachusetts, fully eligible to vote. His livelihood depends on mills and workshops that would suffer economic collapse if the Union fractured; the war's continuation, though costly, seems preferable to Confederate independence. Emancipation and constitutional amendment appeal to his civic sense, though he harbors reservations about the pace and cost of the conflict.

after.quote: The war must be seen through to a proper end, slavery must be done with, but Lord knows how many more boys must fall before we get there.
after.reason: Ernest Reed qualifies to vote under Massachusetts property requirements and will almost certainly cast a ballot as a working man invested in the war's outcome. He leans strongly toward the sitting President's policy of fighting to unconditional surrender and constitutional abolition of slavery, though the war's apparent stalemate and heavy losses give him some hesitation about the administration's management.

before.quote: I cannot vote myself, but my husband will go to the polls tomorrow. I pray he chooses wisely for our sons' sake.
before.reason: Helen Dawson is a woman living in Indiana in 1864, and women do not have the right to vote for president in any state at this time. She is legally barred from casting a ballot regardless of her preferences.

after.quote: I cannot vote tomorrow, though I worry greatly about how this war will end and what it means for my sons.
after.reason: Helen Dawson is a woman in Indiana in 1864, and women are not permitted to vote for president in any state at this time. No circumstance in her life changes this legal bar.

before.quote: I'll vote for the President tomorrow. We've come too far to quit now, and the Union must be preserved whole. The general's talk of negotiation sounds like giving in to me.
before.reason: Walter Graham is a property-holding Pennsylvania farmer whose livelihood depends on preserving the Union and seeing the war through to victory. The sitting President's commitment to unconditional surrender and constitutional abolition of slavery aligns with Union preservation, though Graham may harbor some doubts about the war's conduct and duration given four years of costly conflict.

after.quote: I'm worn out with this war. The General says he'll get us peace without giving up the Union. Four years is enough bloodshed for any country.
after.reason: Walter Graham is a Pennsylvania property-owning farmer eligible to vote. The war's apparent stalemate after four years of heavy losses weighs on him, and the opposition candidate's promise to pursue immediate peace negotiations while still demanding Union restoration appeals more than continued prosecution of an increasingly costly conflict.

before.quote: I cannot vote, being a woman. But my husband will go to the polls tomorrow.
before.reason: Ida Walker is a woman in Iowa in 1864, and women are not permitted to vote for president in any state. She cannot cast a ballot regardless of her preferences.

after.quote: I can't vote tomorrow, being a woman, but my husband will cast his ballot. The war weighs on all of us out here.
after.reason: Ida Walker is a woman in Iowa in 1864, and women have no legal right to vote for president in any state. She cannot cast a ballot regardless of her preferences.

before.quote: I cannot vote myself, though I wish I could make my voice heard on this matter that touches our whole nation.
before.reason: Ruth Robinson is a woman in New York in 1864, and women cannot vote for president. She is therefore unable to cast a ballot regardless of her preferences.

after.quote: I can't vote myself, but I wish I could have a say in this matter. The war has cost us dearly.
after.reason: Ruth Robinson is a woman living in New York in 1864, and women cannot vote for president in New York under current law. She is legally barred from casting a ballot regardless of her political views.

before.quote: The President means to see this through and free the enslaved for good. That general wants to quit and make a deal—I don't trust it will hold.
before.reason: Harry Tate works for wages in an Illinois mill or workshop, qualifying him to vote under the state's property tax requirement. He has spent four years watching the war unfold and will almost certainly turn out tomorrow, but his choice between a sitting president committed to total victory and constitutional emancipation versus a general promising negotiated peace reflects the genuine tension among working men over whether prolonging the war serves the Union or the working people fighting it.

after.quote: The war's gone on long enough with nothing to show for it, but I can't see making peace with slaveholders after all this blood. The Union has to win, proper.
after.reason: Harry Tate works for wages in Illinois and qualifies under the state's property and tax requirements to vote. The war's apparent stalemate and heavy losses weigh on him, but as a working man dependent on steady employment and the Union's industrial capacity, he is likely to support the administration's commitment to unconditional victory and the constitutional abolition of slavery, though the opposition candidate's call for peace creates real doubt.

after.quote: I cannot vote tomorrow, though I wish I could make my voice heard on whether this dreadful war continues another four years.
